notes.content: You know how your grandma used to say, 'Boy, I've been down that road before — don't go that way'? And you stood right there at that corner, you heard her, and you went anyway. That's the image Jehovah draws in verse 16. He says, 'Stand at the crossroads and see. Ask about the ancient roadways, Ask where the good way is.' These aren't hidden paths. He's not asking them to discover anything — He's asking them to ask. But then comes the line that's supposed to land like a gut-punch: 'We will not walk in it.' Not 'we didn't know.' Not 'we were confused.' They read the sign. They put it down. Now connect that to Psalm 25:9 — 'He guides the meek in what is right.' The guidance was there. The problem was posture. So if you're standing at a crossroads this week — a decision, a habit, a relationship — the rest Jehovah offers is already mapped. The question isn't where the road is. The question is whether you'll walk in it.

If you've been wondering whether you're doing something wrong in ministry — that weight you walked in here carrying today — I need you to sit with Jeremiah 6:29 for a second. Jehovah tells Jeremiah: 'The bellows have been scorched. Out from their fire there is lead. One keeps refining intensely simply for nothing.' Now notice what that says. The bellows are scorched — they worked. They burned. Intensely. And nothing came out clean. But Jehovah doesn't rebuke the refiner. He describes the ore. Over in Isaiah 48:4 Jehovah says, 'your neck is an iron sinew and your forehead is copper' — same metals, same stubborn resistance, centuries earlier. The pattern wasn't the refiner's fault then either. So if your neighbor, your coworker, your cousin hasn't responded — the bellows weren't broken. You weren't doing it wrong. The ministry effort you've been second-guessing? That's not evidence of your failure. It's evidence you showed up and kept blowing.
